passage: Gurpreet, you won't believe what I did. You know I've been dying to join the dance workshop? Wanted it for months. Well, yesterday Mummy wrote it into my planner herself. Along with 6 a.m. wake-up, 6:15 yoga, 7:00 breakfast, tuition at 4, dance at 6, "phone off 9 p.m." Every single box filled in, in her handwriting. And I just... said no. To the dance workshop. The thing I wanted! She said, "But Madhuri beti, you begged for this." And I said, "Well, I don't want it now." I went to my room and slammed the door. I've been lying here thinking. I still want to dance. I just couldn't stand that it was one more box she ticked for me. Is that crazy?

qa.q: What did Mummy write into Madhuri's planner?
qa.a: She wrote in the dance workshop herself, along with every other box, from the 6 a.m. wake-up to phone off at 9 p.m.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri say no to the dance workshop she had wanted?
qa.a: With every box filled in someone else's handwriting, refusing was the only way to feel the day was still her own.

qa.q: What could Madhuri say to Mummy that keeps both the dance and a sense of ownership?
qa.a: She could explain calmly that she still wants the workshop, and ask to fill in some planner boxes herself, starting with dance.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel hearing 'I don't want it now'?
qa.a: Mummy may feel confused and hurt, having thought she was helping by booking what Madhuri begged for 😔.

grounding: A teenager whose every hour is planned refuses the very workshop she wanted, to protect her sense of owning her day.

passage: Sudha here. I live across the corridor from Mohit's family, and I tutor him in English on Saturdays. Last week his father pinned a timetable on the fridge: every hour of Mohit's summer, colour-coded. Cricket coaching was on it, at 7 a.m., the thing Mohit had been asking about since March. On Monday Mohit didn't go. Or Tuesday. His father kept saying, "You wanted this!" Mohit only said, "I'm not going if it's on your chart." I don't know exactly what's inside his head. But on Wednesday evening I saw him in the building compound, bowling alone at a chalk wicket on the wall, over and over, until it was dark.

qa.q: How does Sudha see the gap between Mohit's words and what Mohit does?

passage:
Sunaina, you said no to the science camp you begged for, just because I filled in the form. Let me tell you about me at fifteen.
My mother, your Nani, planned my days down to the minute. Wake at 5:30, tuition at seven, school, then painting class at four, 'because you love painting, Nandini'. She even laid out which brushes to take.
And one day I simply refused to go. I loved that class. I'd been saving for new colours. But I sat on my bed and said, 'I'm not going. You can't make me.'
Nani was baffled. So was I, honestly.
It wasn't about painting. It was the only 'no' I had left. When everything is decided for you, even the things you want start to feel like orders.
So, beta. The camp is yours. You fill in the form.

qa.a: At four.

qa.q: Why did young Nandini refuse a painting class Nandini loved?
qa.a: With every minute planned by Nani, refusing was 'the only no' left; pushing back protected a sense that some part of life was Nandini's own.

qa.a: Handing Sunaina the camp form to fill in; giving back ownership makes it easier to want the camp again instead of fighting it.

passage: Pooja, you say you won't go to the dance camp now, just because your mother booked it without asking, even though you begged for it in March. Your Jasleen Bua did exactly that. passage: In their Sector 22 flat in Chandigarh, Vishal's mother had planned his whole summer on a whiteboard: coaching at seven, maths at ten, swimming at four, reading at nine. On Sunday she added one more line in red: cricket academy, from Monday. Vishal had been asking about the cricket academy since January. He looked at the red line and said, 'I don't want it.' His mother put the marker down. 'You begged for it.' 'I changed my mind.' On Monday morning his friend Amandeep came by with his kit bag. 'You coming? Your name's on the list.' 'No,' Vishal said, and shut the door. He sat on his bed and felt strangely satisfied, and then strangely sad. The cricket bag stood in the corner, tags still on. He wasn't sure anymore what he had actually said no to.

qa.a: Refusing felt like taking back some control over his over-planned summer, but he was also sad because he had really wanted cricket.

grounding: A teenager whose whole summer is planned for him refuses the cricket academy he had asked for, pushing back to protect his sense of choice.

“Anjali, wake up. Six-thirty: shower. Seven: breakfast. Seven-fifteen: revise chemistry. Eight: bus.”
“Mumma, I know.”
“Four: swimming. Six: tuition. Nine: bed.”
“I said I KNOW.”

Disha slowly took the timetable down. “Okay. What would you like to plan yourself?”

passage:
The summer I was fifteen, Sarita Masi came to stay, and suddenly there was a plan for everything.
“Kishore, you'll do physics till eleven. Then help me with lunch. Then an hour of reading. Then the cricket camp at five, I've already paid.”
I had wanted that cricket camp for two years. I'd shown Ma the brochure a dozen times.
But when Masi said “I've already paid,” something in me went hard. “I'm not going,” I said.
Ma looked shocked. So did I, a little. I stayed home at five, lying on my bed, furious and bored.
Looking back, it wasn't cricket I was refusing. It was the feeling of being moved around like a chess piece.
The next week I told Masi I'd make my own timetable. I put cricket on it, at five. I went every day.

qa.q: What time was the cricket camp?
qa.a: The cricket camp was at five.

qa.q: Why did Kishore refuse the camp after wanting it for two years?
qa.a: Kishore felt controlled and angry at being moved around like a chess piece, so refusing protected a threatened sense of ownership.

qa.q: What worked in the end, and why?
qa.a: Kishore making a personal timetable; once the choice was Kishore's own, the camp felt wanted again.

qa.q: How might Sarita Masi have felt when Kishore refused the camp she'd paid for?
qa.a: Sarita Masi probably felt confused and hurt, having meant it as a gift.

grounding: The reflection shows a teenager whose every step was planned refusing even a wanted cricket camp to protect ownership.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, Tuesday.
Harsha's mother, Mrs Gopika Rao, came in concerned: Harsha has stopped doing anything she suggests, including the art class Harsha asked for in June. She showed me the family's shared calendar, with every half hour colour-coded by her, including “free time: 7:30–8.”
I met Harsha after lunch. Harsha was polite but tense, arms crossed. When I asked about art, Harsha said, “I did want it. Now it's just another box on Mumma's calendar.” When I asked what Harsha would choose if nobody was watching, the answer came quickly: art, and a walk alone.
My sense is that the refusals are protecting a feeling of ownership more than rejecting the tasks.
Next steps: I suggested to Mrs Rao that Harsha plan two evenings a week without her input, and that they agree on a few non-negotiables together. We will all meet again in two weeks.

qa.q: What did the family calendar list for 7:30–8?
qa.a: It listed “free time: 7:30–8.”

qa.q: How did Harsha feel about the art class now, and why?
qa.a: Harsha felt resentful and controlled, since the class Harsha once wanted had become “just another box on Mumma's calendar.”

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Letting Harsha plan two evenings a week and agreeing on a few non-negotiables together, to give back a sense of ownership.

qa.q: How might Mrs Gopika Rao feel reading the counsellor's view?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and a little hurt, but also relieved to understand why Harsha refuses everything.

Saturday
Mummy wrote my whole day on a sheet and stuck it on my door. 7:00 wake. 7:15 bath. 8:00 maths. 11:00 dance class. 1:00 lunch. Everything, even when to drink water.
I love dance class. I was waiting all week for it. But when I saw "11:00 dance class" on her sheet, something in me went hard. I said I had a headache. I didn't go.
Afreen called at noon. "Where were you? We learnt the new piece!" I felt sick. I wanted to be there so much.
I think it's this: it wasn't my plan any more. Even the thing I love felt like an order. And the only way to feel like me was to say no.
Which is so stupid, because I only hurt myself.
Maybe I'll ask Mummy if I can make my own sheet next week. She can check it.
Neelam
